body:
The spec has never specified the reparsing that legacy browsers did. I think I prefer not having the note in the spec; legacy browsers did all sorts of crazy things that we don't need to document in the spec. The parser is confusing itself as it is. :-)

The new prose seems equivalent, but it's somewhat action-at-a-distance, which I think some people think is generally bad. So my knee-jerk reaction is that we should probably leave this as-is, and maybe just remove the obsolete comment about reparsing.

@zcorpan Agreed about the first part (just thought it would be useful to explain, but even happier not to), not sure about the second. From implementor's point of view, in such form it's much easier to see what steps are needed without repetitive "emit end-of-file" / "reconsume in" noise, which most implementations don't care about anyway (as EOF token is kind of abstract and redundant outside of the spec text).

Moreover - implementors that don't validate HTML (don't emit parse errors), can clearly see and drop any states where EOF action is either "do nothing" or "parse error" without actually checking where all those reconsumptions lead and whether they're important or not (initially I had to dig through the usages of tokenizers to figure out that most of those actions are unnecessary, and I believe many others had to go through this, too).
Maybe it's worth adding a note to that effect about EOF to aid implementers? I tend to agree that not being specific here is less nice.
@annevk Can you please elaborate on what kind of note you mean?

If you indeed meant that whenever the EOF action is "do nothing" or "parse error" the reconsumption lead nowhere (apart from parse error reporting) we could have a note to that effect so that implementers don't have to dig through as you had to do.

@annevk Well, this PR exactly removes those unnecessary reconsumptions and need to dig anywhere. EOF token is mentioned just once in the heading section (where state transitions are described in general), but then throughout the states it explicitly states "do nothing" / "parse error" so that implementors don't need to read any further details or visit cross-references, but do exactly what action states.

I think we should ask parser implementers what they think of the action-at-a-distance question. Right now I know of two active ones, @RReverser and @inikulin :). @hsivonen has also been helpful in such questions and his opinion would be valuable.

Could someone summarize the change so that @inikulin and @hsivonen are able to tell what is being asked about, without having to read the diff?

@domenic The diff is very simple; TLDR: simplify EOF handlers by avoiding repetition of "emit EOF token" and avoiding unnecessary reconsumption steps in those places. That "action-at-a-distance" is executed only once after the entire stream was processed, so can match code even more directly now.

I have a feeling that proposed approach is semantically incorrect. We have "Do nothing." in state if we meet EOF and, meanwhile, we actually should perform some steps described in the section above. So, I will be confused: does "Do nothing" means "ignore everything in `After an EOF character was reached...` section and... do nothing" or does it mean that I should just not perform any actions in current state handler.
Also, action-at-a-distance style is really harder for understanding. It's nice to have as much information "in-place" as possible.

@inikulin What would be the better wording to put here? (so that it doesn't fall into "anything else" case)

Ideally, I think implementations can actually ignore that EOF token as they usually have better ways to know that input has ended apart from fictional one-time token, and it's not even present in html5lib tests. However, for now, trying to change only the tokenization section to simplify things.

EOF character is "action-at-distance" we already have as spec defines that it's not even a character but "a conceptual character representing the end of the input stream", so ideally by adopting such changes we can get to the point where a conceptional character won't be needed at all and implementation can operate directly on the real codepoints.

> Ideally, I think implementations can actually ignore that EOF token as they usually have better ways to know that input has ended apart from fictional one-time token, and it's not even present in html5lib tests. However, for now, trying to change only the tokenization section to simplify things.

But we need formal description for end of parsing and EOF token concept works just fine. 

> EOF character is "action-at-distance" we already have (as spec defines that it's not even a character but "a conceptual character representing the end of the input stream", so ideally by adopting such changes we can get to the point where a conceptional character won't be needed at all and implementation can operate directly on the real codepoints.

It's intentional: tokenizer operates on code points and parser operates on tokens. We need EOF token to maintain this paradigm

> We need EOF token to maintain this paradigm

For the spec clarity, yes. It works well as a concept. But it's not necessary for the real code where you have booleans / functions that already tell the end of stream was reached, and here having "emit end of file token" in section description instead of mixing with real important actions might be useful.

@RReverser I vote for clarity. E.g. from implementer's perspective it's much more sane and both computationally and memory efficient to have 3 token types for character sequences (character sequence, whitespace character sequence, null-character sequence) instead of character tokens for each individual character. But the spec is much easier to read/understand the way it's currently written.

@inikulin Also I think most (all?) real implementations don't have "character" tokens but rather "characters" tokens.

FWIW, I tend to lean on the explicit side: too often people miss things which aren't explicitly defined inline.

> I vote for clarity.

Me too, that's the only reason I'm doing those :)

> much more sane and both computationally and memory efficient to have 3 token types for character sequences (character sequence, whitespace character sequence, null-character sequence)

Well, this is implementation-dependant. As you could see, I've got 30% better speed by not doing so, avoiding non-real codepoints (so that regular string operations would just work) and so on. Anyway, I agree that none of implementation-specific things should be in the spec.

I just thought that having a one action for the originally fictional character, especially kind of action that doesn't affect the validity of execution steps is much simpler than digging through repetitive yet every time slightly different actions for each specific case and figuring out what the differences are, where it leads, why do we need to match that character, and so on because, as I said, I've spent quite a while before figured this out and could reduce size of the codebase by 15% by just avoiding this special EOF character and its handling.

So I'm a bit surprised by the opposition on this one, but if most think that current way is cleaner to understand and work with, then fine.

> As you could see, I've got 30% better speed by not doing so, avoiding non-real codepoints (so that regular string operations would just work) and so on. 

This is pretty interesting BTW - one of the biggest performance boosts in parse5 was achieved by switching to code points instead of strings, since their comparisons are low cost.

> why do we need to match that character, and so on because, as I said, I've spent quite a while before figured this out and could reduce size of the codebase by 15% by just avoiding this special EOF character and its handling.

But we still have EOF and it's handling in states in this PR, but with "distant-action" style. Maybe it just requires some rework which will envolve parser as well, so the whole picture will be much cleaner?
@inikulin what html5lib does is quite subtle: any character that the tree-constructor branches on is emitted as a single character token, but anything else can be concatenated into longer strings
@gsnedders But you will need to re-check character types in parser then. Why do additional job if you already did it on branching in tokenizer? =)
@inikulin oh, we do different types of character token too.
@gsnedders well, it's seems like we do pretty much the same =)

Note that EOF token can also be emitted by `document.close()`, so it's not always a stream of bytes from the network.
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#dom-document-close

> Also I think most (all?) real implementations don't have "character" tokens but rather "characters" tokens.

@gsnedders @inikulin Unrelated to the issue, but thought would be fun to share. I actually found quite a popular implementation that emits each individual character one-by-one as separate token - it's [Google's Gumbo parser](https://github.com/google/gumbo-parser). It never claimed that performance is a goal, but still feels unexpected. https://github.com/google/gumbo-parser/blob/master/src/tokenizer.c#L893-L915
Hmm, I actually have craving to bring this to standard, but it really feels like an implementation-dependent thing.
@inikulin Yeah, I don't think it's worth bringing since everyone does its own kind of handling it.
